title: FCC abolishes gigabit speed goal, suggesting it is unfair to slower technologies
gist: The Carr-led FCC eliminated the Biden-era 1Gbps/500Mbps long-term broadband speed goal and declared current US deployment adequate, dropping price analysis from its methodology despite persistent single-provider markets and Starlink congestion surcharges.

insights.claim: The FCC eliminated the Biden-era long-term 1Gbps/500Mbps broadband speed goal on August 14, 2026, ruling it not 'technologically neutral' toward slower technologies like satellite and fixed wireless.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Removes forward-looking regulatory pressure that favored fiber buildouts, a potential negative for federal-policy tailwinds behind fiber ISPs relative to satellite and fixed-wireless players.
insights.quote: As part of our return to following the plain language of Section 706, we adopt our proposal from the Notice [of Inquiry] to abolish without replacement the long-term goal of 1,000/500 Mbps established in the 2024 Report

insights.claim: The FCC's new report concludes current US broadband deployment (94 percent fixed wireline access at 100/20 Mbps, rising to 97 percent with fixed wireless and 99.7 percent with satellite) already meets the statutory 'reasonable and timely' deployment standard, reversing the prior administration's finding that deployment was insufficient.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: This finding removes the statutory trigger requiring the FCC to accelerate deployment, reducing the likelihood of new federal subsidy or regulatory pushes for broadband expansion.
insights.quote: we conclude our annual inquiry by finding that deployment of advanced telecommunications capability to all Americans meets the statutory standard of being reasonable and timely

insights.claim: Despite the headline 99.7 percent coverage figure, 40.6 percent of US households have only a single wired broadband provider at the 100/20 Mbps benchmark, and 5.7 percent have zero wireline options.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Persistent single-provider markets support a structural pricing-power thesis for incumbent cable and fiber ISPs in those areas, even as the FCC declares deployment adequate.
insights.locator: 40.6 percent of households had just one wired broadband provider

insights.claim: The Carr FCC dropped price and affordability analysis from its deployment report entirely, arguing the statute only requires evaluating 'availability,' while citing industry-lobby-sourced data claiming broadband prices are falling and omitting contrary advocacy-group research.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Signals a lighter-touch pricing-scrutiny regime from the FCC, a modest positive for ISP pricing power and margins.
insights.quote: the 2024 Report strayed from the statute's plain language, which requires consideration of 'availability'—not adoption, affordability, or equitable access.
insights.locator: The Trump-era FCC called that a mistake

insights.claim: The rule change does not affect FCC grant programs like the Rural Digital Opportunity Fund, which still require gigabit-speed deployment in exchange for federal funding, creating a split standard where subsidized rural buildouts must hit gigabit while the broader national policy goal no longer requires it.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Highlights an inconsistency in federal broadband policy that could become a point of contention as more grant-funded networks come online under a different national standard.
insights.locator: Most of the network deployments paid for by the FCC's Rural Digital Opportunity Fund

insights.claim: Commissioner Anna Gomez cited Starlink's 'demand surcharges' of up to $1,500 in high-usage areas to argue that satellite broadband's headline availability numbers overstate real-world service capacity and quality.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Raises a caution flag for using FCC 'covered' satellite-broadband statistics as a proxy for actual reliable service capacity.
insights.locator: Starlink has imposed 'demand surcharges' of up to $1,500
